title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
body:
The theorem the course is named after, and the reason [[Derivative|differentiation]] and
[[Integral|integration]] are taught together rather than as two unrelated subjects. It comes in two
parts and they say the same thing from opposite ends: **these two operations are inverses.**

## Part 1: differentiation undoes integration

$$
\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt = f(x)
$$

Define $F(x)$ as the area accumulated from $a$ up to $x$. Then the rate at which that area grows is
the height of the curve at the right edge, which is obvious once you see it: widen the region by
$dx$ and you add a sliver of area $f(x)\,dx$.

The consequence people miss is that this **proves an antiderivative exists** for every continuous
function. $\int_0^x e^{-t^2}dt$ is a perfectly good function with derivative $e^{-t^2}$; it just
cannot be written with the symbols you know. That distinction (exists versus can be expressed) is
the same one [[Continuity|the IVT]] draws about roots.

## Part 2: the evaluation shortcut

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a) \qquad\text{for any antiderivative } F \text{ of } f
$$

This is the one you compute with, written $[F(x)]_a^b$. **Any** antiderivative works, because they
all differ by a constant and the constant cancels in the subtraction, which is why the definite
integral has no $+C$.

The size of this claim is easy to lose. The left-hand side is a limit of infinitely many
[[Riemann Sum|rectangles]]. The right-hand side is one function evaluated twice and subtracted. A
problem that is genuinely infinite becomes two substitutions and a minus sign:

```
      1                      1
     ∫  x² dx  =  [ x³/3 ]   =  1/3 − 0  =  1/3
      0                      0
```

versus $\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{i}{n}\right)^2\frac{1}{n}$, which is the same
number and an afternoon of algebra.

## The two parts together

Writing $F(x) = \int_a^x f$, Part 1 says $F' = f$ and Part 2 says $\int_a^b F' = F(b) - F(a)$.
Integrate a derivative and you recover the net change; differentiate an integral and you recover
the integrand. **Net change** is the reading that generalises: $\int_a^b F'(t)\,dt$ is the total
change in $F$, which is how a rate turns into an accumulation everywhere from displacement to
probability.

The proof of Part 2 runs through the [[Mean Value Theorem]] applied to each strip of a Riemann sum,
which is where the two halves of the course actually meet.
